::: {.essay-lede}
The Gaussian integral is famous because its antiderivative cannot be expressed using elementary functions, yet its integral over the entire real line has an exact answer.
:::

## The obstacle

We want to compute

$$
I=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx.
$$

Trying to find an elementary antiderivative is not the right route. Instead, observe that the integrand is positive, so $I>0$, and square the integral:

$$
I^2=\left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx\right)
\left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-y^2}\,dy\right).
$$

Tonelli's theorem allows us to combine the two integrals:

$$
I^2=\iint_{\mathbb R^2}e^{-(x^2+y^2)}\,dx\,dy.
$$

## Switch to polar coordinates

In polar coordinates, $x^2+y^2=r^2$ and $dx\,dy=r\,dr\,d\theta$, so

$$
\begin{aligned}
I^2&=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2}r\,dr\,d\theta\\
&=2\pi\left[-\frac12 e^{-r^2}\right]_{0}^{\infty}\\
&=\pi.
\end{aligned}
$$

Taking the positive square root yields

$$
\boxed{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt\pi}.
$$

## The useful lesson

When one-dimensional integration becomes difficult, increasing the dimension can reveal symmetry that was invisible before. Here, a product of identical integrals creates a rotationally symmetric problem—and symmetry does most of the work.
